cases.visibleGeometry: Several irregular knobby highs occupy the upper half, including a compact cluster near the upper right. A faint curved line follows the far right edge; the lower half is comparatively smooth.
cases.alternatives: The knobs resemble exposed bedrock or scattered boulders. The curved line could be a track or field edge. Patchy interpolation around the highs can sharpen their apparent outlines.
cases.supportLimits: The prominent high cluster contains many interpolated cells, so its internal shape is uncertain. Hillshade and local relief describe the same terrain model, not independent observations.

candidates.nextCheck: Inspect original ground returns and wider context to distinguish bedrock from any arranged structure.

cases.visibleGeometry: A narrow, branching north–south incision crosses the patch, with uneven sides and a dark gap near its lower end. Broad rounded slopes descend toward it from both sides. A faint east–west break joins it near mid-height.
cases.alternatives: Likely a drainage or erosion channel, possibly modified by a path, ditch or field boundary. Angular texture along its margins may be model interpolation rather than built edges.
cases.supportLimits: Much of the channel follows amber interpolated cells, and the lower dark gap is missing data. Its cross-section and small edge details need original returns.

cases.visibleGeometry: The central area is smooth, with broad shallow undulations and a faint branching low trending toward the lower left. Small isolated bumps lie near the upper edge and a rougher patch enters at the bottom. No coherent enclosure or platform is apparent.
cases.alternatives: Shallow natural swales, minor rock or vegetation effects, and a change in surface roughness could explain the marks. The upper bumps may be rocks or residual surface objects.
cases.supportLimits: Most central cells are measured, but the small edge highs include some interpolated cells. Subtle relief is near the visual scale of the model derivatives.

cases.visibleGeometry: An irregular, roughly east–west break crosses the lower middle, separating rough upper ground from smoother sloping ground below. A narrow spur projects southward near the centre; several faint diagonal swales feed toward the break.
cases.alternatives: The break may be a natural slope edge or drainage margin, with local erosion and rock exposure. A field edge is also possible. Its jagged appearance partly follows interpolated terrain cells.
cases.supportLimits: Amber interpolation is concentrated along the break and around several small upper highs. The precise edge profile cannot be trusted without checking original returns and broader topography.

candidates.nextCheck: Examine original ground returns and wider context for a continuous constructed bank versus a natural slope or drainage edge.
